source.title: Assessing Inter-Limb Asymmetries in Soccer Players: Magnitude, Direction and Association with Performance

paper.citation: Madruga-Parera, M., Dos'Santos, T., Bishop, C., Turner, A., Blanco, D., Beltran-Garrido, V., Moreno-Pérez, V., & Romero-Rodríguez, D. (2021). Assessing inter-limb asymmetries in soccer players: Magnitude, direction and association with performance. Journal of Human Kinetics, 79, 41–53. https://doi.org/10.2478/hukin-2021-0081
paper.abstract: Do inter-limb asymmetry magnitude and direction differ among mobility, iso-inertial strength/power, and change-of-direction tests, and are asymmetry scores associated with performance? Sixteen semiprofessional male soccer players, age 25.38 ± 6.08 years, assessed in season. Players trained about eight hours per week and had no recent pain, disrupted training, or lower-limb injury under the stated exclusion criteria. Soccer-specific adult male sample; transfer to collegiate American football, women, youth, or injured athletes is indirect. Cross-sectional two-session test battery separated by 72 hours. Tests included ankle dorsiflexion, unilateral flywheel leg extension and leg curl, flywheel crossover step, and 180° change of direction. The sample was powered only to detect large effects (d = 0.98) and correlations of r = 0.60.
paper.tldr: This paper informs how asymmetry magnitude and direction should be interpreted across different testing tasks rather than treated as a single athlete trait. Mean asymmetry ranged from 2.37 ± 1.51% for change-of-direction time to 18.35 ± 12.31% for concentric leg-curl power; all test CVs were below 10% and ICCs ranged from 0.79 to 1.00. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional two-session test battery separated by 72 hours. Tests included ankle dorsiflexion, unilateral flywheel leg extension and leg curl, flywheel crossover step, and 180° change of direction. The sample was powered only to detect large effects (d = 0.98) and correlations of r = 0.60.
paper.findings: Mean asymmetry ranged from 2.37 ± 1.51% for change-of-direction time to 18.35 ± 12.31% for concentric leg-curl power; all test CVs were below 10% and ICCs ranged from 0.79 to 1.00. No player showed the same favored-limb direction across every test, supporting task-specific rather than fixed directionality. Crossover-step asymmetries were associated with selected leg-extension and change-of-direction outcomes, but these cross-sectional correlations do not establish that asymmetry caused poorer performance.
paper.limitations: Small sample with sensitivity only to large associations; smaller but relevant relationships could be missed. The study could not relate laboratory asymmetries to cognitive, perceptual, ecological, or game-specific demands. Iso-inertial loading effects and their transfer to rehabilitation or return to play remain unresolved. Male semiprofessional soccer findings should not be converted into universal asymmetry thresholds for collegiate American-football athletes.
paper.practicalImplications: Use multiple tests when the decision spans different movement qualities, and retain both magnitude and direction by task. An isolated asymmetry score should be interpreted against that test's reliability and performance context, not used alone as a risk label or return-to-play gate.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete development, use multiple tests when the decision spans different movement qualities, and retain both magnitude and direction by task. An isolated asymmetry score should be interpreted against that test's reliability and performance context, not used alone as a risk label or return-to-play gate. Preserve the study population and avoid converting one finding into a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, use multiple tests when the decision spans different movement qualities, and retain both magnitude and direction by task. An isolated asymmetry score should be interpreted against that test's reliability and performance context, not used alone as a risk label or return-to-play gate. This study alone does not establish clearance criteria or a complete return-to-sport progression.
